https://news.tuoitre.vn/hungary-channels.text: Settings Saved news Your Comment Transaction History Logout Saturday, July 18, 2026, 19:03 GMT+7 Hungary channels water to protect UNESCO bird haven amid drought Hungarian authorities have been channeling water into a vast area within the country's Hortobagy National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage site, to ensure its marshlands do not dry out because of this year's severe drought. Lajos Gal, a regional unit manager at the Hortobagy National Park Directorate, walks through the flooded marshland in Hortobagy National Park near Tiszafured, Hungary, July 15, 2026. Photo: Reuters The Hortobagy "Puszta", a magnet for tourists, comprises plains and wetlands in eastern Hungary and is an important stopover for tens of thousands of migratory birds, which build nests and breed here before flying to Africa as autumn nears. The area called "Fekete ret" (Black Meadow) ⁠is the largest marshland and once belonged to the former floodplains of the Tisza river, with its lower-lying parts irrigated by the floods. However, the area dried up for the first time in 2013. Then in 2022, at the time of the previous severe drought, it dried out completely and more than 800 hectares burned down. "Unfortunately, the groundwater level in the area has been continuously decreasing," said Lajos Gal, a regional unit manager of the Hortobagy National Park Directorate with more than three decades of experience working in the marshes. "This is a very special year because the heat arrived very early, and we started the year with a very large water deficit. The spring was not rainy... and the swamp ‌beds could ⁠not fill up. This year we managed to get water from the water department for ecological water replenishment." Gal said about 2 million cubic meters of water have been channeled to the marshes and it is still flowing from the Nyugati irrigation canal. Without this, the entire area would be completely dry by now. Migratory birds affected Climate change and less precipitation have long had an impact, also affecting ⁠birds' migration patterns, he added. "The spring migrations are starting earlier... Since there are no really cold winters, we don't really have to wait for a warming after the long winter and then the spring migration begins, but the birds come back over a prolonged period, ⁠not all at once." He said many species that he would see in his childhood had practically disappeared, but added: "Also, there are species, for example the little pygmy cormorant, which we almost never saw when I was a child, and ⁠nowadays there is a quite nice population here in the Black Meadow." Gal said a long-term solution should be found, and the waters that flow into Hungary should be retained as much as possible to ensure the survival of the wetlands, which also create a microclimate and can influence groundwater balance. https://www.readingchronicle.co.uk/news/.text: History Polish veteran unveils plaque honouring wartime community History By Matt Drake Reporter Share 0 Comments 3 Skip to next photo 1 / 1 Show caption 1 / 1 Share 0 Comments This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. A 100-year-old Polish Second World War veteran has unveiled a plaque honouring the legacy of those who served far from home. Czeslaw 'Ches' Black (Blachucki), the last surviving Polish Second World War soldier in Oxfordshire, revealed the blue plaque at a private ceremony in Checkendon, near Reading, in tribute to the Polish military community that settled in the area after the war. Mr Black said: "Thank you for remembering. "And thank you, especially, for remembering the Polish soldiers who came to Britain, served alongside our allies, and did their part for freedom." Read more Former Flamingos Vintage unit listed for let after summer closure Drivers blasted for illegal parking and blocking paths near Reading hospital Railway bridge closures to deal with 'unstable earth' will disrupt journeys A former employee of Huntley and Palmers in Reading, Mr Black was forced into labour on Hitler’s bunker in Berlin at age 18. He later escaped to Italy, fought with partisans, and then joined the Polish and British Allied forces. He recalled walking through a minefield to save his wounded commanding officer, and in 1947, his unit was relocated to rural Oxfordshire, where he eventually settled. The plaque ceremony brought together descendants from 11 families connected to the former Checkendon Polish camp, including those who endured deportation to Siberia and exile in Africa, India, and the Middle East. Representatives from the Polish Embassy, British Army, and veteran organisations from both countries attended, along with local councillors. A military honour guard was provided by the 7th Regiment, Royal Logistic Corps, based at Dalton Barracks in Abingdon. Royal British Legion branches from Henley, Nettlebed, and Wallingford, as well as Polish Ex-Combatants standard bearers from Reading, also took part. The permanent plaque now installed at The Black Horse in Checkendon aims to ensure that the history of the men, women, and families who lived at the camp is not forgotten. Marian Greczyn, whose father Major Mieczyslaw Greczyn was the camp’s last commanding officer, shared how his father served at Tobruk and Monte Cassino, and how his mother was deported to Siberia with his elder brother, who did not survive. The event was organised by the Friends of Checkendon. Graham Drucker, the group’s organiser, said: "The story is not simply one of military service, but also of the Polish families who made their lives in Britain following the upheavals of the Second World War. "Our Friends of Checkendon regard this event as being the beginning of a wider programme of remembrance. "A further commemoration marking the 80th anniversary of Polish troops arriving at Nettlebed Highmoor is expected towards the end of November and will be open to the public."
